Understanding my cancer diagnosis

A new diagnosis brings a flood of words. You do not need to learn them all today. Start with five facts, write them down, and build from there.

The five facts to ask for

  1. The exact name of the cancerWhere it started (for example breast, colon, lymph node or bone marrow) and the cell type. “Lymphoma” is a family of diseases; “diffuse large B-cell lymphoma” is a diagnosis. Ask for it in writing.
  2. How it was confirmedCancer is usually confirmed by a pathologist looking at tissue or cells under a microscope (a biopsy, or for blood cancers often blood and bone marrow tests). Scans can strongly suggest cancer, but in most cases they cannot confirm it alone.
  3. The stage, or how far it has spreadStage describes size and spread. Some blood cancers use different systems, and some leukemias are not staged at all. See what my stage means.
  4. Biomarker or genetic resultsMany cancers are now tested for specific proteins or gene changes that help choose treatment. Ask: “Were biomarker tests done, and are any results still pending?”
  5. The goal of treatmentCure, long-term control, or comfort and quality of life. The goal shapes every other decision, and it is fine to ask directly.

Your first steps

  • Ask for copies of your pathology report, scan reports and lab results. You have a right to your own records.
  • Bring a family member or friend to visits to listen and take notes. Ask for a medical interpreter if you prefer Spanish or another language; it should be free.
  • Keep one notebook or phone note for names, dates, medicines and questions.
  • It is normal to feel overwhelmed. Most cancers do not require a decision the same day — ask how much time you have to decide.
  • A second opinion is common and accepted. See getting a second opinion.

Call your care team or 911 right away for fever during chemotherapy, trouble breathing, chest pain, sudden weakness, confusion, or bleeding that will not stop.
